paragraphs: I do not mean to refer to all the writers who have written on the subject of female manners — that would in fact only be going over old ground, for they have, in general, written in the same vein. But in attacking the vaunted prerogative of man — the prerogative that may emphatically be called the iron sceptre of tyranny, the original sin of tyrants — I declare myself against all power built on prejudices, however grey with age.

If the submission demanded is founded on justice, there is no appeal to a higher power — for God is justice itself. Let us then, as children of the same parent, if we are not made bastards by being the younger born, reason together, and learn to submit to the authority of reason when her voice is clearly heard. But if it is proved that this throne of prerogative rests only on a chaotic mass of prejudices, which have no inherent principle of order to hold them together, or on an elephant, a tortoise, or even the mighty shoulders of a son of the earth, then those who dare to face the consequences may escape from it without any breach of duty, and without sinning against the order of things.

While reason raises man above the brutish herd, and death is pregnant with promises, only those who have no confidence in their own strength are subject to blind authority. “They are free who will be free!”*
(*Footnote. “He is the free man, whom TRUTH makes free!” Cowper.)

The being who can govern itself has nothing to fear in life; but if anything is dearer to it than its own self-respect, the price must be paid to the last penny. Virtue, like everything of value, must be loved for her own sake alone, or she will not come to dwell with us. She will not grant that peace “which passeth understanding” when she is merely used as stilts for reputation and observed with pharisaical exactness, because “honesty is the best policy.”

It cannot be denied that the plan of life which enables us to carry some knowledge and virtue into another world is the one best designed to secure contentment in this one; yet few people act on this principle, though everyone agrees that it is beyond dispute. Present pleasure, or present power, sweeps these sober convictions aside; and it is for the day, not for life, that man strikes his bargain with happiness. How few! how very few! have enough foresight or resolve to endure a small evil in the moment in order to avoid a greater one later.

Woman in particular, whose virtue* is built on mutual prejudices, seldom rises to this greatness of mind; so that, becoming the slave of her own feelings, she is easily subjugated by the feelings of others. Degraded in this way, her reason, her clouded reason! is employed to polish her chains rather than to break them.
(*Footnote. I mean to use a word that covers more than chastity, the sexual virtue.)
I have listened with indignation to women arguing along the same lines as men, and adopting the sentiments that brutalize them with all the stubbornness of ignorance.
I must illustrate my claim with a few examples. Mrs. Piozzi, who often repeated by rote what she did not understand, steps forward with rolling Johnsonian sentences.

“Seek not for happiness in singularity; and dread a refinement of wisdom as a deviation into folly.” So she dogmatically lectures a newly married man; and to explain this pompous opening, she adds, “I said that the person of your lady would not grow more pleasing to you, but pray let her never suspect that it grows less so: that a woman will pardon an affront to her understanding much sooner than one to her person, is well known; nor will any of us contradict the assertion. All our attainments, all our arts, are employed to gain and keep the heart of man; and what mortification can exceed the disappointment, if the end be not obtained: There is no reproof however pointed, no punishment however severe, that a woman of spirit will not prefer to neglect; and if she can endure it without complaint, it only proves that she means to make herself amends by the attention of others for the slights of her husband!”

These are truly masculine sentiments. “All our ARTS are employed to gain and keep the heart of man:” — and what is the conclusion? — if her person is neglected (and was there ever a person, even one formed with the symmetry of the Medici Venus, that was not slighted?), she will make up for it by trying to please other men. Noble morality! But in this way the understanding of the whole sex is insulted, and their virtue is robbed of the common basis of virtue. A woman must know that her person cannot be as pleasing to her husband as it was to her lover, and if she is offended with him for being a human creature, she may as well whine about the loss of his heart as about any other foolish thing. And this very lack of discernment, or this unreasonable anger, proves that he could not turn his doting on her person into affection for her virtues or respect for her understanding.

While women profess such opinions and act on them, their understandings, at least, deserve the contempt and scorn that men, WHO NEVER insult their persons, have pointedly aimed at the female mind. And it is the sentiments of these polite men, who do not wish to be burdened with mind, that vain women thoughtlessly adopt. Yet they should know that only the reason they insult can spread that SACRED reserve about the person which makes human affections — for human affections always contain some base alloy — as lasting as is consistent with the grand end of existence: the attainment of virtue.
